title: Visual Grounding First, Multimodal In-context Learning Follows
claim: Baselines ground visually and predict correctly with familiar identifiers but fail with novel ones; ours stays visually grounded in both cases.
layout: 2 columns by 3 method rows, top-down; attention heatmaps with colored prediction text
description: The figure is split by a vertical dashed line into two columns. Column (a) uses a generic identifier, "monkey". Column (b) uses a personalized identifier, "Jaden". A prompt bar runs across the top. Beneath it, each column shows two cartoon demonstration images with captions (the identifier is highlighted yellow) and a query image. Three rows follow: Off-the-Shelf, MimIC and ProCoRe (Ours). Each row shows attention heatmaps overlaid on the demonstration and query images, with a prediction sentence below. Correct tokens are green. Wrong or generic tokens ("character", "monkey") are red. In (a) all methods attend to the monkey. In (b) the baselines' attention scatters, while ProCoRe's attention concentrates on the monkey and predicts "Jaden". The eye goes first to the bold red and green words and the heatmaps.
caption: Visual grounding in multimodal ICL with generic vs. personalized identifiers. Attention maps show visual-token attention when predicting the highlighted token using Qwen-VL-3-8B. (a) When a generic identifier (\eg, "{\setlength{\fboxsep}{0.5pt} \colorbox[HTML]{FFE32F}{\textbf{{monkey}}}}") seen during pre-training appears in the ICL demonstrations, both baselines and \ours attend to visual regions relevant to the predicted token (\ie, \textbf{\textcolor[HTML]{318C00}{monkey}}). (b) In contrast, when the generic identifier is replaced with a personalized identifier (\eg, "{\setlength{\fboxsep}{0.5pt} \colorbox[HTML]{FFE32F}{\textbf{{Jaden}}}}"), baselines fail to attend to the relevant region and thereby fall back to generic terms (\eg, "\textbf{\textcolor[HTML]{FF0004}{character}}", "\textbf{\textcolor[HTML]{FF0004}{monkey}}"), whereas \ours correctly predicts the personalized concept (\ie, "\textbf{\textcolor[HTML]{318C00}{Jaden}}") with strong visual grounding. See Sec. [ref] for more examples.
abstract: LLMs have shown strong in-context learning (ICL) capability, but extending it to Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) remains challenging. Prior multimodal ICL methods often rely on ICL-specific datasets for additional training or task vector extraction, which can improve performance on the same ICL benchmark used for adaptation. However, they do not generalize well to other benchmarks and often induce forgetting in previously well-solved tasks. For this reason, we identify 'visual grounding' as the key bottleneck in multimodal ICL; MLLMs often fail to attend to task-relevant visual evidence in demonstrations, instead over-relying on textual cues and producing hallucinated outputs. To address this, we propose ProCoRe to enhance visual grounding through contrastive reinforcement learning on multimodal contrastive data for improving multimodal ICL. ProCoRe generates captions for contrastive image pairs, decomposes them into propositions, and optimizes contrastive rewards that encourage alignment with corresponding images while discouraging mismatched ones. Despite never seeing ICL-formatted training examples, ProCoRe improves average multimodal ICL classification accuracy by 5.6% and captioning ROUGE-L by 13.8% over the off-the-shelf Qwen-VL-3-8B model, outperforming ICL-data-dependent state of the arts across benchmarks. Finally, we introduce PICL, a personalized multimodal ICL captioning benchmark that tests whether MLLMs genuinely understand visual demonstrations rather than relying on pre-trained semantic priors.
